..
Issued at 259 AM CST Fri Nov 6 2026

Early morning GOES water vapor imagery loops show a well-
defined upper-level trough/cut-off low sinking southward towards
the Lower Peninsula of Michigan. As the associated cold pool of
air continues to spill into the lower Great Lakes, a surface 
low meandering around the eastern Great Lakes and an elongated 
surface ridge extending from the central Plains up through 
Hudson Bay will enforce breezy northerly surface winds across 
the region today. The respectable magnitude of this cold air 
advection should largely keep temperatures mired in the 40s 
today with any low 50s readings likely to be few and far between
this afternoon.

The cooler air mass settling into the region will also yield 
15-17C water surface-850 mb temperature differentials and 
6000-9000 ft equilibrium levels over southern portions of Lake 
Michigan today, which will lead to a steady stream of lake 
effect rain showers into portions of southwestern Michigan and 
northwestern Indiana. The predominantly 330-350 degree fetch 
over Lake Michigan should keep most of this activity focused to 
the east of our CWA into La Porte and Berrien counties, but may
still allow for these lake effect showers to affect portions of
Porter County (and possibly far northeastern Jasper County) at 
times through tonight. The aforementioned parameters are also 
marginally supportive of some potential for waterspouts over 
Lake Michigan, though again, the greater potential for this 
should remain focused to our east/northeast along the main lake 
convergence axis.

The Great Plains surface ridge will slide eastward over the 
course of the day today and should be in close enough proximity 
to our area tonight for winds to turn light/calm across a good 
chunk of our CWA after sunset. With temperatures already 
expected to be in the low-mid 40s around sunset and dew points 
progged to mainly be in the low 30s and upper 20s, below 
freezing temperatures will very much be in play for areas 
outside of the core of the Chicago urban heat island and the 
footprint of the lake effect stratocumulus in northwest Indiana 
tonight into Saturday morning. However, some uncertainty remains
with just how much temperatures will fall tonight owing to 
questions about the coverage of any non-lake-induced stratus 
across the area. Most of the latest model guidance favors skies 
clearing out over most our area by the overnight hours, which 
would yield optimal radiational cooling conditions and allow for
temperatures to quickly tank to near or below freezing. 
However, it's not uncommon for stratus to stick around longer 
than depicted in model guidance in these cold cyclonic flow 
regimes during the cool season, and some model solutions, namely
the latest runs of the RAP and UKMET (and presumably the NAM, 
if we still had it -- R.I.P.), do favor an expansive blanket of 
stratus lingering over our forecast area through the night and 
keeping temperatures propped up a bit higher than what is 
depicted in our forecast grids. Note that frost/freeze headlines
for our area have been discontinued for the remainder of this 
fall, but anyone who may still have sensitive vegetation outside
should consider taking the necessary precautions to protect it 
from the cold conditions tonight.

The weather pattern for our area will become fairly benign from
this weekend through at least the first half of next week with 
a split jet stream pattern keeping any real disturbances of note
displaced to both our north and south. A gradual warming trend 
is expected during this time frame with high temperatures likely
to reach the 60s once again early next week before a cold 
frontal passage halts that trend sometime mid-week. Ensemble 
guidance then favors aggregate longwave troughing developing 
over the northeastern quadrant of the CONUS during the latter 
half of the week. If this were indeed to materialize, then that 
could bring about our next chances for precipitation sometime 
mid-late next week, though there is very little ensemble 
consistency at this time with exactly where and when any 
opportunities for precipitation may materialize.

Ogorek
